questions.stem: In electrolysis, positively charged ions (cations) move towards the:
questions.explanation: In electrolysis — cations (+) move to the cathode (negative electrode, hence 'cat' to 'cat-hode'). Anions (−) move to the anode (positive electrode). Opposite charges attract. Mnemonic — 'CATions go to the CAThode'. At the cathode, ions are reduced (gain electrons); at the anode, ions are oxidised (lose electrons).

questions.stem: A common dry-cell (torch) battery uses zinc as the:
questions.explanation: Leclanché dry cell — the zinc CASE serves as the anode (gets oxidised: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻). A carbon rod in the centre is the cathode (where MnO₂ is reduced). The electrolyte is a moist paste of ammonium chloride (NH₄Cl) + zinc chloride (ZnCl₂). As current is drawn, the zinc case slowly erodes from inside. EMF ~1.5 V. Modern alkaline cells (1.5 V) have a similar Zn/MnO₂ chemistry but a KOH electrolyte.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: A lead-acid battery, used in most cars, has an electrolyte of:
questions.explanation: Lead-acid battery — Pb (anode) / PbO₂ (cathode) / ~30-40 % H₂SO₄ (electrolyte). On discharge both electrodes convert to PbSO₄; concentration of H₂SO₄ drops. Charging reverses the reaction — which is why car batteries can last many years with the engine's alternator recharging them. EMF 2 V per cell; 6 cells in series give the 12 V car battery.

questions.stem: Electroplating a metal object with silver involves making the object the:
questions.explanation: The object to be plated is the CATHODE (attracts Ag⁺ cations from the silver-nitrate / silver-cyanide electrolyte; they get reduced to Ag and deposit on the surface). The anode is typically a slab of PURE silver — it gets oxidised, replenishing the Ag⁺ in the bath. Used in jewellery, decorative cutlery, printed circuit boards (gold plating).

questions.stem: Which battery technology is dominant in modern smartphones and electric vehicles?
questions.explanation: Lithium-ion (Li-ion) — high energy density, light, rechargeable thousands of times. Cathode typically LiCoO₂ or LFP (lithium-iron phosphate); anode graphite; electrolyte a non-aqueous lithium-salt solution. EMF ~3.6-3.7 V per cell. Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2019 went to Whittingham, Goodenough, Yoshino for Li-ion development. Ni-Cd is older technology (has toxic cadmium; being phased out). Lead-acid is still dominant in ICE cars. Zn-C is a non-rechargeable dry cell.

questions.stem: Galvanisation — to prevent iron from rusting — involves coating it with:
questions.explanation: Galvanisation = coating iron or steel with zinc — either by hot-dipping or electroplating. Zinc protects iron by 'sacrificial' oxidation: even when the coating is scratched, the zinc corrodes before the iron. Tinning (tin coating — used on food cans) is different; tin merely blocks oxygen but does not give sacrificial protection. Applications — roofing sheets, wire buckets, pipes, rebar.

questions.stem: Faraday's first law of electrolysis states that the mass of a substance deposited at an electrode is directly proportional to:

options.option_text: The time the current is applied squared

questions.explanation: Faraday's 1st law — m = Z × Q = Z × I × t, where Z is the electrochemical equivalent, I current, t time. Q = charge passed = I × t. Faraday's 2nd law — when the same Q is passed through different electrolytes, masses deposited are in proportion to the equivalent masses. 1 Faraday (96,485 C) will deposit 1 mole-equivalent of any species. These laws are exam-favourite application questions.
